SPACE SURVIVAL MISSION 

ASTRO MASTERS is fun space game made with scratch by KAREEM, YASSIN and MARYAM. 

In this game,an astronaut goes on a space mission for more than one day.

The player must help the astronaut stay safe by managing five important resources:

*Oxygen 

*Food 

*Water 

*Energy 

*Shield 

All resources start at 79%

The player must keep them at safe levels by solving 

Challenge and making smart choice
summary:
# Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
**Introduction:** This project teaches students how astronauts live in space through a 48-hour mission with Mariam and Karim.
**Space:** Astronauts float in orbit and need oxygen and protection from extreme temperatures.
**Spacesuits:** Spacesuits provide oxygen, control temperature, and protect astronauts.
**Recycling:** Astronauts recycle water, produce oxygen, and clean the air.
**Daily Life:** Astronauts use special food, sleeping bags, and toilets. They secure objects so they do not float away.
**Health:** Space can weaken muscles and bones, so astronauts exercise for two hours daily.
**Mission Plan:**
- Hours 1–12: Check the spacecraft.
- Hours 13–24: Practice hygiene and recycle water.
- Hours 25–36: Exercise and do experiments.
- Hours 37–48: Observe Earth and finish the mission.
**Sources:** NASA STEM, Gamoras Space School, Orbital Radar Aerospace Briefings, and HowStuffWorks.
**Conclusion:** This project teaches students about space, science, teamwork, and astronaut life.

Project Details: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Hackathon & Challenge: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer Team: Astro Masters Team Members: Mariam Mohamed El-Nattar & Karim Eslam Abdelaziz

1. What does it do or how does it work?

The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational framework and training curriculum designed to teach children and young learners the science, technology, and real daily survival skills needed for space exploration.

The project operates through a simulated 48-Hour Spaceflight Mission Timeline divided into core operational phases:

  • Hostile Environment Simulation: Contrasts Earth’s hospitable 1G atmosphere with low Earth orbit’s vacuum, microgravity (continuous free-fall), and orbital temperature swings (+121°C to -157°C).
  • The Spacesuit as a Personal Spaceship: Breaks down the 14-layer Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU), explaining its hyperbaric 4.3 psi pure oxygen system, liquid-cooling garments (LCVG), primary life support system (PLSS) carbon dioxide scrubbers, and emergency SAFER propulsion.
  • Closed-Loop Resource Recovery: Demonstrates circular survival systems, showing how station life support reclaims 98 out of every 100 drops of water from sweat, breath moisture, and urine, and uses electrolysis to generate breathable oxygen.
  • Daily Living in Microgravity: Teaches practical adaptations—eating crumb-free tortillas instead of bread to protect avionics, drinking liquids through one-way valves, using liquid salt/pepper suspensions, sleeping in wall-tethered compartments, and utilizing airflow suction toilets.
  • Physical Countermeasures: Explains physiological adaptations like spinal decompression (growing up to 5 cm / 2 inches taller) and enforces the mandatory 2 hours of daily resistive exercise (ARED and cycle ergometers) to stop bone demineralization and muscle atrophy.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Demystifies Space Science: Moves beyond superficial space trivia to teach authentic aerospace engineering, bio-regenerative life support, and human physiology in simple, relatable terms.
  • Fosters Scientific Literacy & Systems Thinking: Helps students understand how air, water, and energy interact in closed systems, demonstrating practical conservation on both spacecraft and Earth.
  • Promotes Health & Discipline: Connects astronauts' mandatory daily workouts and nutritional discipline with healthy living habits for kids on Earth.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to spark STEM curiosity and empower young students—particularly elementary and middle schoolers—to see themselves as future astronauts, engineers, and scientists. By casting two relatable junior commanders, Mariam and Karim, as mission leaders, the project makes space exploration feel inclusive, accessible, and achievable for youth around the world.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Design & Visual Prototyping: Graphic design tools and digital illustration software for character modeling, mission badges, and the visual identity of Astro Masters.
  • Presentation & Pedagogical Authoring: Presentation software to engineer the structured 7-slide mission briefing with custom futuristic UI styling.
  • Data Synthesis & Aerospace Research Tools: NASA Open Educational Resources, NASA STEM Engagement portals, and technical flight documentation (EMU schematics, ECLSS reclamation telemetry, and space hygiene engineering data).
  • AI & Workflow Orchestration: Collaborative agentic AI workflows to synthesize complex technical manuals into a cohesive 48-hour youth-oriented training syllabus.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Character-Led Storytelling: Rather than presenting dry technical manuals, the project anchors every technical concept to Mariam and Karim, guiding trainees through hands-on challenges and relatable scenarios.
  • "Your Spacesuit is a Spaceship" Mental Model: Re-conceptualizes a piece of clothing as an independent, pressurized aerospace vehicle with thrusters, cooling radiators, and atmospheric scrubbers.
  • Gamified Mission Arc: Transforms life-support maintenance, hygiene, and workouts into an engaging 48-hour mission log where trainees earn their Junior Astronaut Wings by solving orbital challenges.
  • Engaging Space-Vessel UI Aesthetics: Pairs cockpit-inspired, high-contrast visual styling with friendly, vibrant visuals to deliver complex science without intimidating young audiences.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Age Appropriateness & Cognitive Load: Distilling advanced hyperbaric physics (e.g., 4.3 psi pure oxygen vs. 14.7 psi atmospheric mix) into intuitive explanations without losing scientific rigor.
  • Technical & Scientific Accuracy: Strictly adhering to real NASA International Space Station operational data and physiological research (e.g., bone mineral density loss rates, closed-loop water recovery metrics, and orbital thermal limits).
  • Safety & Hazard Awareness: Highlighting why seemingly minor terrestrial habits (like eating crumbly bread or shaking dry salt) turn into critical life-support hazards in microgravity.
  • Global Educational Accessibility: Structuring modules so they can be adapted into physical classroom activities, digital interactive apps, or printable mission logbooks anywhere in the world.
